blocks.x: I'll just start it right off and ask you your name. I'll get you ready. What's your name? Lawrence Trump.
Now that they just go, we're getting the second reel of Lawrence Tribe. So, anyhow, you were saying you had those big bands going in. How many nights a week would you all work?

Well, we'd work long, twice a week. And did you work days then? Well, I had a little job then. It wasn't too much. When I was with Celestan, I didn't work because, well, I was single. And I was just in a band just to say I was, you know, had a lot of publicity then, you know, in the band.
But you had to work when you were with Robert Clark, I bet, to make it on. You couldn't make it on one or two nights a week.

You know, because most of those fellas were in there. Going to school, Clyde Kerr was in school. Ewan was in school. William Houston was in school. So, the school boys. Well, I had a little job working.
You were not asking what you did? Oh, no.
I was working, at that time, I was working at a grocery store. Oh, no. I was working at a grocery store. Oh, no. I was working there. I was working there. In the grocery.
You've done a lot of things there, no? A lot of different.
That's right. To try to make it.
Yeah. Well, you have to. That's right.
I like this. I worked at this, on this jeepney job. About a year and a half with Handy. Mm-hmm. At La Vida.
Did I ever tell you that? I worked there.
No, but I heard about the job. You heard about it?
Yeah, but I don't know that much about it. Who was in the band?
When we were at the La Vida? Yeah.
Handy, you said?
Handy. Jim Robinson, trombone. Mm-hmm. Benny Turner, playing piano. Mm-hmm. I was playing drums. Sidney Flosier, playing guitar banjoons.
Did you have a bass?
No bass.
No trumpet?
No trumpet.
No trumpet at all. What was Handy playing?
Playing alto. Oh, yeah.
Was he playing any clarinet at all?
He was playing plenty clarinet then. Oh, yeah. But now, I don't think we're with it.
Oh, yeah, he's come back. He can do it now. He can do it again. On the clarinet? Yeah. Finally, he's ready, you know. And he came out with it. He sounds good. Maybe not as good as he did then, but...
He could play plenty clarinet. Mm-hmm. Plenty saxophone, too.
Yeah.
Yeah, see. That's where I got that hard leg from playing with Henry. He'd make a drummer strong. Why is that?
Why is that?

Well, he sort of like to, you know, break in. If you solve anything, you get hard playing with him because he played long numbers he would play. It would help, you know, a drummer. Yeah. It helped me playing with fellas like him.
Yeah. Did you have to play many fast numbers?
A lot of fast numbers. They were short, but they, you know, jitney.
What did you play the jitney? What else besides the fast numbers? How would the job go? Would you play any waltzes?

Yeah, they'd play waltzes. It makes many. Slow numbers, fast numbers, waltzes. They'd play two choruses. Mm-hmm. See, jitney, that's what they used to do. Taxi dance, they call it. You know, they'd go and take a nickel a dance. That's what it was then, you see. See, when they'd get through with that chorus, they'd take down. That's it. And they'd go again.
I don't see how he made it. That must have been awful hard on them.

With no trumpet, huh? He made it. Because he used to pick up, hand it, pick up all those numbers. He could play hand it, play hard. He'd play hard. He was a good man. Play him and Jim Crow. They were blown.
Well, I guess they had iron whips. They were just iron men for that kind of job. That's right.
They wanted to be family. They could make it.
What time did they start in the morning? I mean, at night, what time did they start?

See, I think we were playing either 8.30 or 9, but I know it was daylight before I'd get home. Play in the morning, you know, until the morning. I just remember the time. You know, it was late and we'd get off. Did they pay you? Fifteen dollars a week.
Did you consider that good money then? It was a good thing. What year was that? How do you? What year was that? What year was that? What year?
That must have been around in the 30s or the 40s. It was somewhere around there.
Was it before the WPA drawback?
I believe that was before.
Well, first was Robert Clark and then you went on to who? We can get it straight now.
We were Celestan after Robert Clark. I was with Robert Clark. We were Celestan last.

And Celestan was the last band player? The last band. And then Handy and the WPA were in between. That's right. And Huntley-Guardette? Was with us? No, I mean you played some jobs with him too. Oh, I did play jobs with him. Yeah, but that was after Robert Clark. That's right.
Another place I forgot to tell, I played there a long time ago, the Rhythm Club. I played back there at Jackson and Durban with Henry Russ.
What was Russ playing?
Russ was playing trumpet.
Oh, yeah. I never ever heard him play trumpet. I don't know. Maybe once or twice when he was playing bass with Thomas or something.
And Crump, Isidore Crump, he met him.
No, I never have met him.
He was playing alto.
I know there was a Frank Crump that played saxophone. Do you know that one again? Frank Crump? No.

He died. I think so. Frank Crump, I think was a little bright fella. Frank died. Isidore Crump, he still live in. He has a what? He has a jurist. Oh, really? Yeah. How big a band did Russ have? Russ had a ten piece band. Man, you played with nothing but big bands for a long time. I played. I had a good bit of experience with them. You know. I had experience with them.
Because if I played, I'm not bragging, but if I played with any of them, you know, I had
experience with them.
Because if I played, I'm not bragging, but if I played with anybody once or twice, I would

get hired again. They would hire me. Well, when you were playing with somebody like Robert Clark or something or that, would you be out in the field too, taking other little jobs on the side? Well, I would when I was playing with somebody like Robert Clark or something or that, would
you be out in the field too, taking other little jobs on the side?

Well, I would when I was playing with them because, you see, Robert Clark was considered an organized band, but with Hunter Gaudet, any of the fellas that wasn't considered an organized band, it's just a group has gotten together. If they get something, we go and play. If you get something, I'll go and play with you. That's how that's done. A lot of spots, huh?
That's right.
And we would make it like that.
You'd have a gig one night here and a gig one night there. That's it.

During those times, practically every musician had something to do. It was small, the money was small, but you were working. It looked like you enjoyed playing. Wasn't getting nothing much because we were single. We would make two, three dollars and so like that. We just spent it up, you know, just had fun and pleasure. Sure, you just want to tell the truth about it.
Oh yeah, you could lose money on a job, man, huh? In some ways, I guess, huh?
That's right, because we didn't have no family. Probably if I had a wife and children, I wouldn't, you know, do that. But single, just having fun.
Sure.
Make two, three dollars and just spend it all. No, I was going to work the next night. Yeah. That's how that was.
Well, people had a good time then, though. Even though it was tough times, people still had a good time, huh? They had a good time.
And it seemed as though everybody was happy and in good evening.
Mm-hmm. Well, sometimes when you know what you're up against and everybody's together, that makes it easier. That's right. I guess.
Oh, man. In fact, every little joint around you had four and five pieces.
Mm-hmm.
Every night somewhere, they had four and five pieces in each place, playing. Mm-hmm.
Did you have any favorite drummers then, as you began to get on with more experience with any more you liked?
Besides Bob Rand?
Yeah, Bob Rand and different people you heard. I mean, either in personal or on records or anything? Radio?
Well, I had another fellow I used to like. Mm-hmm. His style was a little different, but I liked that beat he had. That was Roy Evans. Mm-hmm.
Who was he with then? Roy Evans played with Sam Morgan. Oh, yeah.
David Jones had a six-piece band. Poin-el played alto.
You heard of him? Yeah.

You heard of him? Called him Wiggles. Well, he made a record with David Jones when they were at the Astoria. Is that the same time? Same. That's right. Did you ever hear Lee Collins? Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Lee Collins. Lee Collins was playing trumpet. Oh, yeah?
Oh, yeah. Joe Robichaux was playing piano. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Roy Evans was playing drums. Did they have a guitar or anything like that?

Sales from him. Sales was playing bamboo Roe Rovershaw was playing piano. Roy Evans was playing drums. Did they have a guitar or anything? Sales. From him, Sales was playing banjo. I know him. Sales. Where's he now, Sales?
I don't know. I think that's manual sales. He's in Chicago.
Roy had a beat. He was a kind man. I liked that beat he had. I liked his drumming.
Did he do anything special that you could describe?

Whether he had a beat he would use on his foot, I don't know. It was just different than most drummers. It seemed as though it was like a skip. A skip beat or something. He'd beat a four-fourth rhythm and he'd sort of skip in between. It was just a little... I guess that was a secret. It was something. I tried to catch that, but it looked like I couldn't get that.
Is it anything like they do on the street, the brass band bass drumming? Is it something like that?
Something on that order. It was a slight difference. Maybe by being an orchestra. It would sound a little different.
What did he do with his hands? Did he have anything special to help that beat along?

Nothing. Just ordinary. He'd be playing. Using his sticks. He'd be playing. Did he have roles or cymbal work? He had a role. He had a technique in using the tom-tom. He'd use his tom-toms differently. He'd make different beats on the tom-tom.
Did he make many of explosions and things like that? Sometimes. I don't know. Who did you listen to in the street? What drummers did you hear in the street?
Well, now, my drummer, I used to listen to in the brass band was a little fella by the name of Jim. Jimbo. Call him Jimbo.

Is he any kind of the hog? The guy they call the hog? I don't know. You don't know the hog? I don't know. Know who? The hog. The hog? Who's the hog? This guy's name was Mewkes. He used to play with the Eureka for a while. This guy, he's an old, short, fine-skinned fella. Did you ever know Black Benny? That was before your term, I guess.

I don't remember him. I think he died before I... Well, he and the hog were buddies, isn't it? Sure enough. The Black Benny is supposed to have been a great face drum, but I never heard him. I haven't either. I heard a lot of talk of him that he was. The Jimbo was my ideal. Brass. Brass band. What did he look like? I think I knew him. Little short fella, smiling all the time. Always smiling. And he had a beat and had a skip. And he beat that bass drum. He beat it.
And I think I heard him. I think that must be Jim Mewkes. He must be. He really has to be. He's dark, huh? Jimbo? Yeah. He's dark. Yeah, I know.
I don't hear no other drum beating a drum like that. No, I haven't heard it since.
Do they have any good snare drum in the street?
Happy. Happy. Good snare drum, man.

You know, I'm tired of hearing the Saints, but any time I heard him play that in the street, that was something. You know, the leaves. He'd build that up. Boy, he could really play it. Ooh, Happy. Happy, yeah. Happy.
You know, he'd really play like something. Yeah, Happy. It's a good snare drum. Mm-hmm. Yeah. Yeah, see?
Yeah, I'm getting back to something I meant to ask you about before. Who played before you were the Handys band? Do you know who the drummer was? Before I played? Yeah.
Roy Evans. He was in that band. Roy was in that band and Kimball, old man. Kimball was playing bass.
Mm-hmm. But you didn't play with Kimball then? In that band?
No, I didn't play. Mm-hmm. I see. See, I was Handys big band in Louisiana Shakers. Oh, that was before he went in La Vida, huh? Hmm?
No, I mean, there was a, I thought maybe you took somebody's place at La Vida.
No, that was after, see, Handys had a short band there, La Vida.
Yeah. And then he had a big band?

He had a big band before. Oh, before. That's when Kimball, man, Kimball was playing bass. And Roy Evans. Yeah. And I know the trumpet player was playing with him. Clifford Brown was one of the trumpet players. Mm-hmm. A fella, I know him well, he played in the WPA band. He's dead now. That was the trumpet player was playing with him. Raymond Brown played trombone with Handys. Bartley played third alto.
Who is Bartley? What's his name? I don't know.
Bartley, he's dead now. He's a nice alto player.
You know, there's one guy I've been trying to trace up and that's the drummer they call Papa. Did you ever know him? Mm-hmm. Years ago.
Yes, I remember him. I'm wondering what happened to him.
I think I may have seen him once or twice.
Papa. Sort of Indian color, the olive color, something like that. I remember him. I don't know what the name was. Wavy hair. That's right. That's the guy I'm talking about. That's right.

I don't know what happened to him. I haven't seen him. It seems to me he held his sticks funny, too. Yeah. Maybe he held both of his sticks like that. Yeah, yeah. Instead of, you know, both of them straight out instead of cupping the one in his left hand. That's right. That's the guy. That's the same guy I'm talking about.
That's him. I don't know what became of him. Mm-hmm. That's right. I do remember him. Yeah. I just wondered what became of him. Mm-hmm.
Did you tell me all about Rush at the Rhythms Club? I've forgotten. I think we got off the subject there, too. We're rhyming tonight. One thing, another.
Yeah, there were so many things come up, you know, and it used to make you think of a lot of different things. Mm-hmm. We were talking about Rush. You asked...
Yeah, who was in the band.
Who was in the band, and I named some of them. Isidore Crump was one of them.
Mm-hmm.
Earl Barnes was playing, isn't it? Earl Barnes.
Mm-hmm. Earl Barnes. What instrument did he play?
He played tenor, sax. Walter Daniels playing piano.
Well, if you can't think of them, don't worry about it. You know?
Yeah, some of those fellas I've forgotten. Yeah, that's been a long time. Yes, I've forgotten some of them.
How many nights a week would you have to work in the Rhythms Club?
We had a cocktail hour every Sunday. Mm-hmm. And I think we had one or two nights a week, but we had the cocktail hour every Sunday. Yeah. Cocktail hour was sitting around here, maybe we heard of it.
Mm-hmm, yeah.
Yeah, well that's...
What time would that be?
That would be four o'clock. Mm-hmm. Four to nine. Mm-hmm.
Were you playing any parades then?
I wasn't playing any parades.
When did you start playing parades? I don't know. Recently? Yeah.
See, I have it down here. Yeah.
You mean not until July the 26th, 1964? That's your first parade at the Cornerstone Land in Gretna, huh?
That's the first parade. Yeah.
Well, I'm thinking. So in the old days, you didn't play many parades then? I didn't play many parades.

That group, I don't know, it seemed as though the fellas that were older than what we were, they were taking over the parades, they wouldn't hire us. Mm-hmm. You know, we wouldn't have a chance at the parades. That's the way it was then, you know. Yeah.
Did they have any good arrangers in around New Orleans? Anybody could write arrangements?
They had some good arrangers around here. Mm-hmm.
Well, what did y'all use in the band? Did you get stock arrangements or did you use all special arrangements or what? They mixed them up.

Henry Holloway was arranger for the Sellers Stand Band. Mm-hmm. Kildee, we called. Yeah. He did all the arranging. Mm-hmm. And Clyde Cub was arranging a little more than Houston then. Mm-hmm. And he arranged some.
Is that with Robert? Robert Clark.
Robert Clark. Robert Clark. Robert Clark. Mm-hmm. Those two did the arranging. Yeah.
Well, did they have any, would you say their arrangements sounded like anybody else? I mean, were they pretty much swing arrangements at the time or? They were swing arrangements.
Mm-hmm.
Did any of them sound much like Duke, like, or, or, or, or, or, or, or Basie or what?

Something similar. They arranged, uh, the arrangement would be, uh, sort of close to them. Whatever number that they would play, it seemed as though they would try to arrange it as close as they could to that particular thing.
You mean like, if somebody had a hit record? Mm-hmm. So they, they, they'd try to catch it, huh? That's right.
Because, uh, Clyde Cub used to arrange from records.
Mm-hmm. And arrange it exactly like the record one would.
Oh, my God. Clyde Cub, yeah. That's what I think about Don Albert.
He sounds, a lot of times he sounds like Duke Ellendon to me. Mm-hmm. Even the solos and everything.
So, that's right. Mm-hmm.
You'd think it's Harry Conney and Barney Begad and Cootie Williams. That's right. You'd hear the record.
Yeah, the record and arrange from the, uh, the record. Yeah. Yeah.
They'd get the style of gun packs on those guys. That's right. She put smoking down. Yeah.
You smoke cigars?
Uh-huh. Just that. They don't want to smoke every time. And in the car, too.
Mm-hmm. Yeah.
Well, anyhow, uh, I don't know. I don't know.
I don't know.
I don't know.
I don't know.

I don't know. I don't know. I don't know. Uh, who do you think was the best arranger here? I hate to put you on the spot like this. Or would you say you like one any more than the other? Well, I think they all were good. Mm-hmm.
They were good arrangers.
Mm-hmm. Yeah. Because I'll never hear that now. You know, not much of those. There's not much left of those now, the way big bands are in arrangements here.
I haven't heard Euston's band in a long time. Mm-hmm. I don't know what style they're playing on now. And I don't know how they sound.
Well, Larry's band is still up, huh? Larry's band is up.
Mm-hmm. And they play a lot of rock and roll. Mm-hmm. I haven't heard them.
Because I was asked to join that band.
Mm-hmm. And then, both. Do you like rock and roll? I should be versatile, but I don't care for rock and roll. I just don't like it.
Mm-hmm. What about rumbas and things like that? Do you like them? I like rumbas.

I used to play a lot of rumbas when we were playing with different bands. I mean, with different fellas. But places we played, now they haven't been asking for rumbas. The last rumbas I played was a project. I played at Charity Hospital. Mm-hmm. Were you there that night?
The night I brought Dizzy's bass player off? Yeah, did we play any rumbas that night? I think so, maybe. I don't remember.
And didn't they have some young lady that asked for rumba and she got out there and was dancing?

Yeah, I think so, that's right. They had some Spanish girls. Spanish, that's right. American girls. Well, that's the last time I played, remember? Playing in the rumbas. Mm-hmm. Well, was dancing different in the 30s then? I mean, they had many other dances besides rumbas and that. What did people do then?
Well, that breakaway they called it and different things like that. That swing out, you know, throw the gun out and swing out like that, you know.
Was that like the Big Apple at all? A pecking or a jitter bugging?
Something nice, something similar. Yes, something similar. Okay. Were you playing any of what they called Dixieland now in that time?
Was it 30? Well, I think so. Mm-hmm. That is, you know, the group of us. I don't think we've gotten away from that style of playing.

The only thing now, I think my style is a slight different because I used to use a lot of wire brushes then. And I used wire brushes then. And I used wire brushes. I used wire brushes. Less now than I used to. Yeah. asked for a lot of wire brushes. The leaders or the dancers? Some of them. The leaders would. That just kept you away from the sticks. But now they're using more sticks now than wire brushes. Wire brushes is used in some numbers because the other night I was asked to use wire brushes on Satan Numbers. Whose band was that? Allison Roof. That was his job, you know, and he asked. I've been playing quite a few jobs with him. Who does he use usually? He has you? Joe Harris. During the summer he was using his cousin on organ. But he's a rock and roll man. I don't know him. Lester. His name is Lester. He plays organ. Is his name Lester Anderson or do you know him? I don't know his. I'd have to look in the book. It's in the book. It is. Does he have a guitar player? No. Trombone. Trombone. Who, Anderson? Well, when he went to Pensacola he used a trombone. And he used Onus in Pensacola. They used Kimble the other night. On guitar? Banjo. Banjo. That's not in Kimble. The young Kimble. That's right. And Ernest Rueblow he used for both. To Pensacola. Who did he have on trombone over there? Frog's son. Oh yeah.
Gerald Joseph. That's right. And he has Joe Harris on the alto. Alto. And he must be using piano now if he doesn't use it at all. Piano.

Yeah. Sing didn't go with us this year. I've forgotten this fella's name. Some fella from downtown he used on piano. But ordinarily he has Sing Miller. Sometimes. Sometimes. He's playing with Kimble now. Miller is. Oh really? He plays with Kimble. I didn't know that.

Yeah, I should ask Charlie Hamilton about that. I saw him the other day when they opened the bank in the National City Bank. Charlie Hamilton was there. Charlie Hamilton was there. Or you was there too? Yeah.
Oh, did I record that?

No, we just turned it on. I thought we want to get everybody's name on here. We got Lawrence Trotta, and this is the third reel. Let's get your name down. Who are you? So they'll know when they hear this.
I wonder what's my background. My background wasn't bad, but I've been working all my life.
Your name.
Your name? Ernestine.
Trotta, huh?
Trotta.
And you've known him a little while?
I have known him up. How long, Lawrence?
He's asking you.
Oh, oh, yeah. That's right. That's good. We've been married about 15 years. We met in church. Statenau's Baptist Church.
I just wanted people to know who you were, you know, when they hear this. That's his wife always picking on him. That's right.
Well, my name is Betty Rankin.
And I'm Dick Allen. Hi, everybody.
Boy. Where you going to put that on the what? On the radio?
No, we keep this up at Tulane. We keep this up at Tulane, so.
I ought to go on the television.
But, you know, when he gets to be a famous drummer in England now, I saw his name in a magazine all the way from England today.
Today? Today. Tell me what magazine I did. It's called the Jazz Times.
Yeah, yeah.
Am I talking again?
Well, it's something, yeah. It's something Plyde wrote up, the trumpet play, Plyde Wilson.
I remember when he'd taken that note from Lawrence.
So now that you got famous, someday people come and listen to this, you know. Oh! I know.
What magazine would that be in?
Jazz Times.
Where can I get it? Newsstands?
And Clive would get it.
Clive would get it from me.
Great. He'd get it. So you get to see it.
Oh, great.
Yeah.
I hope that would be on the cheap, huh? Yeah.
What about? We never didn't get into Solestad's band. You never didn't tell us about that band.
You mean all the men in the band? Yeah.
And what you did and where you went and so on?
We went on to the state of Texas, Arkansas, Mississippi, Alabama. Texas, Mississippi, Alabama. Yeah.
I did.
You got around then with Solestad, huh? I did. Was he well known out in those little country towns?
Well known. That's right.
I always thought of him as being more famous around here. I know you used to get good work here.
He used to get a lot of work through different states.
Mm-hmm. Well, did he get good pay then? I know that. And during those times?
Well, during those times, the little money we used to get. It was considered, you know, good.
And you said you could live off that money, huh?
Certainly living off that money. Because I was single and some of the men had wives. But I didn't have any.
How many wives? I don't know.
He said wives. He didn't say wives.
He said some of those men had wives. I know they gonna have kids. When I move my latch, you know.
Yeah, I know. Well, I have no musicians. I have no musicians who married a different wife every time they went to. You know, that happens, too.
I didn't have one. Kid.
You didn't worry about that. Kid. You went to Kildee was in there, huh? What was he playing?

Trumpet. Second trumpet. Gaudet was playing first trumpet. Celestine was playing third. You have a trombone player? Bill Matthews was playing trombone. Tom Johnson was playing first alto. Willie James Squeak was playing third. Cyclone and Clarence Hall was playing tenor.
Squeak is from here. Where is he from?
Squeak is from here. That's Willie James. That's Louis James' nephew.
I see.
Adam Kiddo was playing piano. Joe Lawrence was singing. Kimball was playing string bass. John Porter was playing. John Porter was playing suzer for me.
He had two of them?
Two basses.
Like one, two? Which Kimball was that?
No. Kimball?
Not the only man. They don't remember. Yeah. Guitar?
He was playing string bass.
No, did they have any guitar in there? Didn't have no guitar. Oh, I see. Yeah. Well, did this guy Lawrence do all the singing or did anybody else sing?
Just him would sing. Mm-hmm. He played a sock and a washboard. Oh, yeah?
And a washboard.
Mm-hmm.
Did he play them on every number or would it be featured or what? How did that work?
Satan numbers he played, the washboard. And sweet numbers, some waltzes he played a sock.
Mm-hmm. How did the washboard go with it? Did the people like that?
Well, they seemed to like it.
Yeah, I guess that'd be a novelty, something like that. That'd be something different.
That's right. That's right.
Do you remember what numbers he played for washboard? No, I really haven't.
I can't remember the numbers.
What kind of tunes would you be playing then in the big bands anyhow? Would you play in Dixieland or polkas or waltzes or the hit tunes, pop tunes?
Well, they were playing popular tunes at that time. There were popular tunes, waltzes, rumbles.
What did Pampas Alistair do? Would he just sit in a second and read or would he get it?

That's all. He would be featured in this number, My Josephine. That was his number, you know. He would feature him in that number. Muscat rambled. Didn't he rambled? Numbers like that. They'd feature him in those numbers. Did he sing then? He sang. I just understand, sang a number. I've forgotten the name of that number. He used to sing. He did used to sing a number. I've forgotten.
Did he get up and dance or shake it around on him then?
No, he just sang.

He's quite a chord towards the end then he'd get up and have his little act. Yeah. I know you had some of them doing that stuff. Yeah. I know. What about the other bands? Did they feature any different special numbers? Any original numbers or anything? You know, ones they wrote themselves? Well, they would.
They'd feature numbers. Mm-hmm. Numbers.
Was there anybody around who was really good at making up numbers there? No. I don't think so. I know there's… Sometimes some of those arrangers have their own original numbers, you know?
All that, but not so much then, huh? I don't know. Maybe too much. Yeah.
What about those Kato's? Yeah.
What about those Kato's?
Yeah. I don't think so. I don't think so. Mm-hmm. I know there's… Sometimes some of those arrangers have their own original numbers, you know? But not so much then, huh? No.
Not too much. I don't remember too much. That's… What about those Kato's?
Can you tell me now? Adam was one, huh? Adam. Mm-hmm. There was a cousin, Jimmy Kato. He died. Well, the Kato's played more house parties.

He didn't play with too many bands. He played with a few short bands. That's Jimmy. That's Jimmy. Yeah. That's Jimmy. Yeah. That's Jimmy. That's Jimmy. The big man. Yeah. The first cousin to Adam. Mm-hmm.
And what about Adam's father? Did he play? Can you tell me a question?
I think his father played drums. I don't remember him, but I think his father played. You didn't know him. I didn't know him. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
Can you think about anything actually about those early days? Okay. I don't worry about it. When did you stop playing? I stopped playing in 46. Mm-hmm.
Mm-hmm. Why'd you stop? Should I ask?
Is that a secret? Yeah.
Huh? That could be all right. What? Why'd you stop?
Why'd you stop? Or should I ask?
Is that a secret? Yeah. Don't tell him that's an old thing.

Huh? Because that could be all right. Why? Why? It would be all right. Why? But that would make the other musicians feel bad. Because he went back to church. Oh. And he thought it was a sin. Mm-hmm. And the lady that I was working for told him it wasn't a sin.
What church was that you do?

Uh, St. Mark. Baptist. That's right. I was working, working in the church, you know. I had more time, you know, I didn't have too much time than to work. Working on the trustee board and I had to be there at all times, you know, on the go, working. That's mostly the reason why I didn't have too much time.
Well, do you think it's a sin to play music?
I don't think it's a sin.
Mm-hmm. To play jam? I don't think so. Not now.
He doesn't think so. But it's all closed and stuck on my mind.

Okay. Well, yeah, a lot of guys playing in church, you know. Like Harrison Bonds is your name right now. That's right. I know trombone. Yeah, and Little Jim plays in his church now. Bass player. Yes. I see him. Very nice. But did you have anything to do with music after that? After 1946? You completely put it down? I put it down. I wasn't playing at all. And did you see any other musicians there or anything?
No, and then I used to see them.
You didn't go around listening or did you?
See, I worked on the boards, you know, in the office there. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. He wasn't playing at all.
And did you see any other musicians there or anything?
No, and then I used to see them.
You didn't go around looking or did you?

Well, I didn't go around looking. In fact, I mostly, I devoted most of my time to the church by working in there. See, I worked on the boards, you know, in the office there. And I had to be there at all times, you know, take care of where the finance was, you know. I worked on the trustee board.
Did you ever do any preaching?
Preaching. No preaching. No preaching.
How long did you work on the trustee board?
From 46 until… 46 until…
63, I think. And that was the only job you had or did you do anything else at all?
Well, I worked on another job. I worked, but I was just working there in the church, you know. There wasn't no pay in there. Just giving my service there.
And what did you do during your regular job? What kind of job did you do?
What kind of work I'm doing now? I worked at DH Holmes, a part of that.
What did you do? Chinese people worked there, you know that? Who was that? There's a man who used to study drums from Chinese, that name, Hugh Evans. Oh, the President? The President was at home.
The President. Yeah. Did you know that? I didn't know that.

He was a Chinese pupil. He wanted to be a drum. I think, boy, that he didn't have to be president of DH Holmes. That's what they said. He loved it. Yeah, it's easy. I didn't know that. Well, he and Harry Sushant are good friends. I think that's what Harry told me about. He loved drumming and loved Chinese playing. Hmm. Well, anyway, when did you come back?
Why did you come back? Why did I come back?
Yeah, why did you come back?

Well, I met Willie Humphrey one day on the bus. He and I began talking and he said, Why didn't I come back to play? He said, you know that I could play, always could play. So, he said, look over your mind and think about it. I think less than a month I had made up my mind. I called him and told him that I had it in mind. He said, well, that's good. I just went on and got set of drums and started out. And that was the first that I see I have. I moved down there.
Did you have to join the union to play that drum?
Oh, I had to join the union.
Yes, I had. Were you in the union before?
No, a lot of us wasn't in the union because the union wasn't anything then.
Even Celestan's band, huh?
That's right. A lot of those brothers, they weren't in the union. No.
Well, could union and un-union musicians play together then?

Yes, because you didn't hear much union talk then. The only thing they wanted to know if a man could play, if he was capable enough of holding a job to get him. They didn't ask him, was he in the union or anything like that.

You didn't have to prove that you had paid up or anything? Didn't have to do that then. Let's take a look at your book so that we can talk about that. You've got everything you've written down about it.
Yeah, I just used to write that stuff.
Let's see. Here. Your first job was a cornerstone line in the Grapnel. In July 26, 1964, I mean. You said that's when you made your comeback, huh?
That was it. Yeah.
And what band was it?
That was Minor. I played with Minor.
The triple player? Anderson Minor.
Goody. Anderson Minor.
Mm-hmm. Okay. And then did you play many more? Let's see, we've got September the 4th, Gulfport.
I played there with Octia. Mm-hmm. Octia Crosby. Mm-hmm.
And then October the 17th, the Harmony Inn.
I played there with Anderson and Harold Desjunt. Harold Desjunt.
What was that? Piano player?
Harold Desjunt.
No, I said, was there a piano player down there? Do you remember?
Sing.
Oh, yeah. Then I covered the 26th, Tulane University.
That was with Anderson and Joe Harris.
I don't guess I knew anything about that. It was on December the 5th, 1222nd Street.
You remember that? Mm-hmm. That was one of yours. Yeah, I was there. You gave us that one.
Yeah. Let me see, who was in the band? Three pieces, huh?
Me, Ernest Rubelow, and Octia. Yeah, Octia.
Yeah, that was a lot of fun. That's right.
We had some fun that night.
Yeah. I don't remember it too well. You don't remember it too well? You remember me bragging about that, Ernest?
Yeah, that's right there, can that rehearsal. Oh, a year ago.
Yeah. Let's see, and then December the 12th at American Legion, I regret it, was that a dance?
It was a dance. That's Morgan's job, Andrew Morgan.
Mm-hmm. December 15th, Charity Hospital.
There was a project with Arubanet, Leroy Arubanet, you know his?
Yeah, the Tenant Club.
That's right. That's right. That was his job.
Mm-hmm. Is he in the union? Was he in the union? Yeah. I didn't know that. I didn't know whether he was in the union.
He's in the union.
Mm-hmm. Who did he have in his band? Do you remember?
Mm-hmm. That night? Mm-hmm.
They had Joe Bentley.
Mm-hmm. You know Big Father Al? Mm-hmm. Father Al was playing with us. Mm-hmm. You know Albert DeLong? Yeah.
Albert DeLong.
Mm-hmm.
Sing. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.
That night was playing trumpet and Albert DeLong playing alto. Mm-hmm. And Father Al played guitar. That's right.
Mm-hmm. He had six of us. Yeah. And then New Year's Eve, Pensacola, Florida, huh? That's right. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. That was Anderson's.
Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm. And they had, go ahead.
They had, go ahead.
They had, go ahead. They had, go ahead.
They had Ernest Rublo, Joe Harris, and they had Showboy that year. Mm-hmm. That was in 60.
64. Yeah. Yeah. They had, they had the showboy that year. Mm-hmm. That was in 60. 64. Yeah. That's right. Mm-hmm.
January was low, not in that month. That's in 1965.
That's 65. And then February, the 16th, Charity Hospital again. That's right.
Charity Hospital again, that must have been. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Either, uh, Morgan had a project or Octave. Mm-hmm. I think you was up there. Yeah.
I think that's the night. Joe Bentley was there.
I think so.

Yeah. And, uh, I came up with Chris White, the bass player from Dizzy's. That's right. Okay. And Rublo was playing Dying Job. Mm-hmm. And, let's see, Joe Bentley. That would be it, unless it was a trombone. I don't think it was any trombone, no. Warner. Warner, that's right, yeah. Because I remember Chris White liked Warner and Rubio playing. That's right. And then March the 2nd, the parade at the Corner Club. You were there. Mm-hmm. I got notes on that, I guess. That would have been Anderson's band, Anderson Mount, I remember.
That's right. Because you remember you asked me, who were some of those fellas, say you didn't know them, are they in the union? Yeah.

Yeah, some of them, you know, I'm always seeing new people at parades. And good people too, you never know who's going to turn off. That's right. At a parade. In March the 16th, you were back at Charity.
That's right.
I wonder what band that would be. Yeah. I wonder if you can't remember. I can't remember. It's one of those.
Let's see. No, I don't think that would be Tillman's project.
No, it would be. That was later, Tillman. Tillman was sick then, huh?
Yeah. In March.
Yes, that's right.
Yeah. That's right. Yeah. That's right. Yeah. That's right. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
That's right. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. That's right. It wouldn't be. Because his was a little later. Mm-hmm. His was not so long ago. Wasn't it? John Joseph.
I mean, John Joseph. John Joseph. And somebody didn't. They all go and one went on one side and one went on the other side.
Well that's the night Father Al played with that Rubinette. That's the night John Joseph.

And the night I was there, when I brought the bass player up with me, they had Kimba on the other side. You remember some of the guys came over, Jesse Charles? That's right, that's right. You know, it's at our law. Sure.
The man that died. You know the musician that died, it might have been him up there.
It might have come down town.
Wasn't he up there in there?
That's Marine, is that on there?
Yeah, we're coming to that. Oh, I'm sorry. April 23rd, 8031 South Robertson.
Yes, that's somebody's job. Let's see now. This trumpet player, John L. recommended him to me. I can't call his name. That was his job.
But it's where up in Carroll, you know.
That's up around the school then.
Yeah, 8031 South Robertson, it's right near Carroll.
Yes, remember that night I threw in a big... Was it a party or a dance or what? It was a party and a house.
House party.
House party.
And June the 6th, Lucha, Louisiana.

Lucha, that was Anderson's job. June the 6th, must have been a picnic. Mm-hmm. Did you play many picnics in the 30s? Not too many. Not too many. Not too many. I played too many picnics. Mostly my playing was, you know, like these little gigs around these little nightclubs. I played plenty of nightclubs. I played in practically every place here in New Orleans. You know, the Rhythm Club, New Orleans Country Club. Well, I played there with Celestine, but I'm just saying practically all these little nightclubs I played in. Cali, Enter, the Opera House and all those places. I played in all of those. That's where my work was mostly done around there then, you know. Then up here they had this Seventh and Howard Grand Terrace, I told you, and the Black Gold and all those places. But I didn't play too many picnics. Now, we used to advertise on trucks then. I did a lot of that. Advertising, but I didn't do no parading, but advertising on the trucks.
Did they have big bands on the trucks or short bands? Short bands. About hundred and a pieces.
About five or six pieces like that. You ever buck? Yeah, they probably had.
Who'd you meet up with?

Well, sometimes, like I'd be with a hand there, would be on one and Rene would be on it and his brother would be on the other. See, Rene was living there in a trumpet player. And his brother Joe would be on drums. And he had a saxophone player named Edgar Socia. I don't know if you heard of Edgar Socia. I heard of him. Yeah. Henry Harden, that was a tenor player. Meet up fellas like that, you know. They'd be on one truck, we'd be on another. How did Rene play then?
Oh yeah, he played nice trumpet. He played nice, yeah. And Alvin would be on the truck sometime too.

Alvin Alcorn, cause he was playing with Tyrone. Alvin used to play a lot on the short bands, cause he always was using Alvin. He was a good man, you know. Always used to use Alvin. Would Hange use a trumpet on the trucks? Oh yes. Who'd he get on the trumpet? Well, sometime he'd have Alvin with him, sometime he'd have Clifford.
He used to use Clifford Brown, Raymond Brown's son. Clifford Brown. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Clifford Brown.
I never had known what Clifford Brown sounded like.
I never heard him. Never heard him. Did the trumpet players ever copy Louis Armstrong? Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm.
Did the trumpet players ever copy Louis Armstrong down here then?
Well, they had some trumpet players around here used to copy. I think Lee Collins was trying to play something like Lee Collins.

I'll never forget one night I heard him at the paddock and he played, I think it was, I may be wrong on these tunes. When you smile and then he turned it over and played whatever tune was on the other side. I could see the record in my mind some of these days or whatever it is. I just knew that he had the Louis record. That's what he was doing. That's right. You get the feeling when he played it just like Louis. Just like Louis. Just like Louis.
He was a nice trumpet player.
What did Clifford Brown sound like? Did he sound like anybody you remember?
I don't know. Look, Clifford Brown had a kind of style of his own. He didn't play like nobody else. He had a style of his own. Yeah, it's such a hard thing to tell.

That's right. But you know, it's not fair. Like you think you know what somebody sounds like when you listen to a record, but that's not always fair. When Renee made some records, all he did was play straight lead in the middle register, you know. But I know he could do more than that. Sure. Because I heard him once in person myself. You did? Yeah. Yeah. And he got off that too, I want to tell you.
Yeah, see, he was a nice trumpet player. Yeah, he was a fine trumpet player. When I heard he was fading, you know, it was towards the end.
When you heard, yeah. Yeah, it was around 47 or something. Oh yeah. So I don't guess he was at his best. No.
Not that time. That's right. It was fading, you see.
Let's see, back to this. June the 20th, 1965, you have St. John Parade. What is that?

You was out there too. You remember when we played, our Grand Lodge met here, St. John Grand Lodge. See, I'm of that jurisdiction. And I happened to be in one of the bands. That's the Masons. The Masons, that's right.
Did you end up at Booker Tee? Is that the damn big of a boy? I got those things confused.
We were at the ILA. Oh yeah. Remember when we were?
You had a few bands out there. That's right. That's one of the biggest parades I've ever seen in my life. I saw. Yeah, that was you.
That's right. They had about six bands, huh? Yeah. Something like that. Yes. Yeah.

And let's see. I think we're about to run out of this tape. So we can put another one on. We can get it. Knock off one. I'm going pretty easy. I think. Huh? Yeah. I hate to get in the mouth of anything. And stop. And it's just...
Well, you're doing real well again. Sorry. I'm trying to.
This is real folk, huh? Lawrence Trial. We'll go on, you say that was your lodge, St. John.
St. John Grand Lodge. United Most Wishless St. John Grand Lodge.
Well do you belong to many societies?
Only one Masonic Lodge.

segments.title: Interview opening
segments.summary: Allen starts the recording and asks Trotter his name.

segments.title: Work schedule and day jobs during the big-band years
segments.summary: Trotter says he worked a couple of nights a week with Celestin and Robert Clark and held a grocery job while single; schoolboys filled the bands.

segments.title: The jitney dance job with Handy at La Vida
segments.summary: Trotter lists Handy's small band at La Vida (Robinson, Turner, Flosier, no bass or trumpet) and says the long, fast numbers hardened his leg.

segments.title: How the taxi-dance job ran: hours, pay, dates
segments.summary: Two-chorus numbers at a nickel a dance, playing until daylight for fifteen dollars a week, around the 1930s-40s before the WPA cutback.

segments.title: Order of bands: Clark, Handy and the WPA, then Celestin
segments.summary: Allen and Trotter straighten out the sequence of Trotter's bands.

segments.title: Henry Russ's band at the Rhythm Club
segments.summary: Trotter recalls playing at the Rhythm Club with Henry Russ's ten-piece band and its sidemen, including the Crumps.

segments.title: Organized bands versus pickup gigs; small pay and good times
segments.summary: Clark's was an organized band while others were pickup groups; single men earned two or three dollars a night and enjoyed it, with small combos in every joint.

segments.title: Favorite drummer Roy Evans and his skip beat
segments.summary: Trotter admires Roy Evans, who played with Sam Morgan and David Jones, and describes his skip beat and tom-tom work.

segments.title: Brass band drummers Jimbo and Happy
segments.summary: Trotter's ideal bass drummer in the street was Jimbo; Happy was a fine snare drummer; Black Benny is discussed.

segments.title: Who played in Handy's big band before La Vida
segments.summary: Handy's earlier big band, the Louisiana Shakers, had Roy Evans, Kimball and Clifford Brown, Raymond Brown and Bartley.

segments.title: Remembering the drummer called Papa
segments.summary: Allen and Trotter try to place the olive-complexioned drummer Papa who held his sticks oddly.

segments.title: Henry Russ's Rhythm Club band personnel and the Sunday cocktail hour
segments.summary: Trotter names Isidore Crump, Earl Barnes and Walter Daniels and describes the Sunday four-to-nine cocktail hour.

segments.title: Parades: first parade in 1964, older men took them earlier
segments.summary: Trotter did not play parades in the old days; older musicians took them, and his first was July 1964.

segments.title: Arrangers and copying hit records
segments.summary: Henry Holloway and Clyde Kerr arranged for Clark's band, swing charts modeled on records by Ellington, Basie and others.

segments.title: Opinions of current bands and rock and roll
segments.summary: After off-topic chatter, Trotter says the arrangers were all good, mentions Larry's band and says he dislikes rock and roll.

segments.title: Rumbas and 1930s dances
segments.summary: Trotter used to play rumbas, last at Charity Hospital, and describes breakaway and swing-out dances like the Big Apple.

segments.title: Dixieland, wire brushes and Anderson Minor's current band
segments.summary: Trotter says his style hasn't left Dixieland and discusses wire brushes, then who plays in Anderson Minor's group and the Pensacola trip.

segments.title: Third reel: Ernestine Trotter introduced and the Jazz Times mention
segments.summary: New reel; Ernestine gives her name, says they met in church and married about fifteen years, and Allen mentions a magazine item about Trotter.

segments.title: Touring with Celestin and pay in those years
segments.summary: Trotter says Celestin's band toured Texas, Arkansas, Mississippi and Alabama; the money was good enough for a single man to live on.

segments.title: Personnel of Celestin's band and the singer who played washboard
segments.summary: Trotter lists the sections of Celestin's band and says the singer played washboard on hot numbers and sock cymbal on waltzes.

segments.title: Repertoire and Celestin's featured numbers
segments.summary: The band played popular tunes, waltzes and rumbas; Celestin was featured on a few numbers and sang, with few original tunes.

segments.title: The Kato family of musicians
segments.summary: Trotter says Adam Kato and cousin Jimmy Kato played house parties and a few short bands; Adam's father may have played drums.

segments.title: Quitting music in 1946 for the church
segments.summary: Trotter stopped playing in 1946 because he thought it a sin; he devoted himself to the church and its trustee board.

segments.title: Trustee board, his day job at D. H. Holmes, and a drumming executive
segments.summary: Trotter did no preaching, served unpaid, and worked at D. H. Holmes, where Allen says a company president studied drums.

segments.title: Willie Humphrey persuades Trotter to return
segments.summary: Willie Humphrey talks Trotter into playing again; Trotter buys drums and returns.

segments.title: Joining the musicians' union
segments.summary: Trotter had to join the union on his return; earlier many players, even in Celestin's band, were not union members.

segments.title: Trotter's gig book: first jobs after the 1964 comeback
segments.summary: Going through his book, they cover the July 1964 job with Anderson Minor and later jobs with Octia Crosby, Joe Harris and Andrew Morgan.

segments.title: Charity Hospital projects, Pensacola and the Chris White night
segments.summary: The book lists Charity Hospital jobs, the Pensacola New Year's job with Anderson, and the night Allen brought Dizzy's bassist Chris White.

segments.title: More 1965 jobs: parade, house party, Louisiana picnic
segments.summary: Trotter and Allen run through jobs from March to June 1965 and try to recall bands and leaders.

segments.title: Few picnics, many nightclubs, and advertising trucks
segments.summary: Trotter mostly played nightclubs around New Orleans and did advertising truck jobs with short bands.

segments.title: Trumpeters on the trucks: Rena, Alcorn, Clifford Brown and Armstrong imitators
segments.summary: Trotter recalls bands on the trucks with Kid Rena, Alvin Alcorn and Clifford Brown, and Allen and Trotter discuss trumpeters copying Armstrong.

segments.title: St. John Grand Lodge parade and Masonic membership
segments.summary: Trotter describes playing the 1965 St. John Grand Lodge parade with his Masonic lodge and says he belongs only to that lodge.
